claims.text: The base multi-component high-entropy alloy tends to crystallize under typical quenching conditions.
A minor boron addition of approximately 1–3 at.% can promote glass formation in a high-entropy alloy.
Boron addition enhances atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Boron addition enhances topological frustration in the alloy.
The boron-induced size mismatch and topological frustration inhibit crystallization during rapid cooling.
Rapid quenching by melt-spinning or splat cooling can be used to process the proposed alloy.
Boron produces increased atomic-packing disorder and local structural frustration.
The increased disorder and frustration result from boron's size mismatch and strong chemical interactions with metallic elements.
Boron atoms are small relative to the metallic constituents and have metalloid character.
Boron disrupts regular atomic arrangements and introduces additional topological constraints.
The topological constraints introduced by boron slow the nucleation of crystalline phases.
Boron increases the undercooling required for crystallization.
Increasing the undercooling required for crystallization enhances the alloy's glass-forming ability.
The boron-modified alloy will have a higher critical cooling rate for crystallization than the undoped alloy.
The boron-modified alloy will have a greater tendency to form an amorphous structure than the undoped alloy.
Too little boron may have only a minimal effect on glass-forming ability.
Excessive boron may cause crystalline boride phases to form.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says boron inhibits crystallization and enhances glass-forming ability, but the predicted outcome specifies a higher critical cooling rate for crystallization. If this means crystallization remains possible at faster cooling rates, it opposes the claimed inhibition. Enhanced glass-forming ability is ordinarily framed as a lower critical cooling rate needed to avoid crystallization, so the stated metric is internally ambiguous or reversed.
